messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 50
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Animator
- Trauma Type: Child's life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 70

When he talks about the beginning of it, he does not start with the diagnosis. He starts with a Tuesday afternoon at his animation studio, sitting under the bluish light of two large monitors, adjusting the timing of a character’s expression frame by frame. His phone vibrates once, then again, then a third time. He almost ignores it because he is in the middle of a deadline and because his wife rarely calls repeatedly unless something is wrong. By the time he answers, he can hear panic in her breathing before he understands any of the words. Their son has collapsed at school. The ambulance is taking him in.

He remembers the drive to the hospital in fragments: red lights, the smell of stale coffee in his car, his hands slipping on the steering wheel because they are sweating so badly. In the emergency department, everything becomes both too sharp and unreal. He sees a doctor kneeling to speak to his wife, sees a nurse running with a tray of supplies, hears the monitor alarms, and cannot make any of it fit into a story his mind can tolerate. His son, who had seemed healthy that morning, is suddenly surrounded by tubes and strangers speaking in urgent, clipped sentences. He stands there feeling useless and ashamed of how badly he needs someone to tell him what to do.

The illness unfolds over days and then weeks in the pediatric ICU. There are complications, frightening swings in hope, and long stretches when nobody can promise that his son will survive. He sleeps in a chair beside the hospital bed, if he sleeps at all. He starts measuring time by oxygen levels, by rounds, by the hiss of machines. He watches every movement of his son’s chest. When the boy’s breathing changes even slightly, his own body jolts as if an electric current has passed through him. Family members call from overseas with prayers and advice, and he answers mechanically, stepping into hallways to speak in a calm voice he does not feel. He notices that he is no longer eating unless someone puts food in front of him. In the mosque, where he goes once during a brief break, he finds himself unable to pray in a steady way; his mind keeps returning to the image of his child’s face under fluorescent lights.

His son survives. This is the fact everyone around him holds onto, and for a while he tries to live inside it. There is a discharge home, medications, follow-up appointments, and a slow return to ordinary routines. Friends tell him how lucky they are. He says yes, we are very lucky. But his body does not seem to believe the danger is over. At night, when the house finally quiets, he hears again the monitor alarms from the ICU. Sometimes he wakes convinced he has missed a call from the hospital, his heart racing so violently that he has to sit on the edge of the bed and press his palm to his chest. If his son coughs in the next room, he is up instantly, already imagining the worst before he opens the bedroom door.

Before the illness, his work as an animator had been a place of absorption and pleasure. He liked the patience of it, the tiny decisions that give movement emotional truth. Now the screens exhaust him. He finds himself staring at a sequence while his mind replays scenes from the hospital with cinematic clarity: the plastic tubing taped to his son’s skin, his wife crying into her scarf, a physician saying, “We have to prepare for all possibilities.” He loses hours to these memories. Sudden electronic beeps from editing software make him flinch. When coworkers joke that he seems jumpy, he smiles tightly and says he is just tired.

At home he becomes watchful in a way that strains the whole family. He checks his son repeatedly while he sleeps. He asks too many questions about headaches, stomachaches, fatigue. His wife tells him gently that he is hovering, that their son needs room to feel normal again. He knows she is right, yet each time he tries to step back he feels reckless, as if vigilance is the only thing standing between his child and catastrophe. He becomes irritable over small things—unfinished homework, a missed phone call, dishes left in the sink—and then feels guilty almost immediately. His daughter has started avoiding him when he is in one of these moods. He notices this and hates himself for it.

He also avoids. He takes longer routes to avoid driving past the hospital. He cannot watch medical scenes on television. He leaves the room if relatives begin retelling the story of how frightening that year was. During one family gathering, an aunt says, “At least that is all behind you now,” and he feels a flash of anger so intense it surprises him. Behind us for whom, he thinks.

In sessions, he is composed at first, even polished, with the reflexive steadiness of someone used to holding other people together. Then, when he describes standing beside his son’s ICU bed, his voice thins and he looks past the room as if he is seeing it again. He says he should be grateful, and he is, but gratitude sits on top of something rawer: a constant sense that disaster is waiting just outside the frame. He has spent his career creating motion from still images. Now he feels trapped inside a handful of images that will not stop moving.
